attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: 'I fully expect' is an unqualified expectation, so it counts as a scored forecast. The 12-month horizon converts correctly to July 28, 2025.

contract.note: Reading 'begin to burst' as the start of a broad, sustained unwinding of investment and valuations is ordinary and fair. It correctly excludes brief selloffs and treats falling deal counts with rising value as concentration, not a burst.

evidence.note: Independent EY measurement: H1 2025 GenAI VC of $49.2B already exceeded all of 2024. Fewer deals reflects concentration, not contraction. Published before the cutoff.
S&P webinar page dated July 15, 2025. It gives a qualitative view of continued funding momentum near the deadline, which corroborates e1 but is not a measurement.

reviews.rationale: The deadline has passed. Sector investment reached a record in H1 2025, above all of 2024, and July commentary shows momentum continuing. Fewer deals points to concentration, not a broad sustained contraction. The contradiction condition is met, although valuations were not measured directly.

attribution.note: Marcus's own bullet point, listed as one of his reasons.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim about the competitive state of generative AI suppliers. The normalisation keeps the universal 'nobody'.

contract.note: The broad business meaning of 'moat' is an ordinary reading. Whether incumbents' existing distribution advantages count is the contract's choice, not Marcus's, and a model-only reading could change the result. The July 2024 window is reasonable.

evidence.note: Joint statement from four competition authorities, July 23, 2024; it is really the primary text, not a secondary summary. It frames incumbents' accumulated advantages as a risk and makes no company-specific finding of an established GenAI moat.
Meta's own disclosure that Llama is competitive with frontier models. An interested source that speaks only to model capabilities, not to other kinds of advantage.

reviews.rationale: Neither item establishes that a named supplier had a durable generative AI moat in July 2024, and neither shows that no supplier had one. The regulators describe risks, not findings; Meta's statement is interested and only about models. The evidence settles neither condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assessment in his post.

semantics.note: An existence claim that GDM's July 2024 work shows neural and symbolic parts can be usefully combined. 'Contra Hinton and LeCun' is correctly left unscored.

contract.note: Context supports reading 'profitably' as technically useful. The support condition asks only for neural-symbolic interaction producing valid proofs, which matches the words.

evidence.note: A coauthor's account, published before the cutoff, that the RL-trained proof network searching in Lean produced the IMO 2024 proofs for P1, P2 and P6. This is a developer account, not an independent finding.
Feb 2025 AG2 preprint describing the language-model and symbolic-engine interface. A later architecture description, used as context only.
DeepMind's published Lean proof artifacts from July 2024. They are machine-checkable formal outputs from the AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry agents; problem statements were formalised by hand.

reviews.rationale: The primary proof artifacts and the developer's account show neural models working with formal symbolic machinery (Lean and the deduction engine) to produce valid proofs of hard IMO 2024 problems. That meets the existence claim. Hand formalisation of the inputs does not defeat the claim under the contract. Sources are first-party, but formal proofs can be checked.

attribution.note: Opening sentence of Marcus's own post.

semantics.note: 'Will soon flame out' is a firm forecast with no fixed date. The contract keeps the 'won't completely disappear' qualifier.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to borrow the 12-month deadline from the next sentence and treats 'soon' as having no endpoint. Reading 'flame out' as a substantial, sustained collapse is ordinary.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure from June 2026 reporting adoption growth. It weighs against a collapse so far but cannot settle a forecast with no deadline.
Independent Reuters Institute survey: weekly generative AI use rose from 18% to 34% between 2024 and 2025. Growth, not collapse.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. The evidence shows continued growth, not the sustained collapse the early-resolution rule requires. Under the contract, growth at a given date cannot conclusively refute an open-horizon forecast, so the claim stays unresolved.
